Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

AITA for not wanting to include the foster kid in a family photo? | This will be on a throwaway. I’m hoping Reddit can help me solve a dilemma between my siblings and I. I am the second oldest of 5 siblings. We are 21 M 19F (me) 16F, 13M 9F. Every year since my youngest sister was born we have been doing funny photo shoots for my mom’s birthday. We put the photos into a giant card and all go out shopping for her birthday present. This has become a tradition that has gotten better and better over the years. My Mom always loves it and collects the cards. Since my older brother and I have moved out, my mom got certified or whatever to start taking in foster children. They have one (14 or 15ish? F) that’s been staying at the house for like four months. Here’s the dilemma: I don’t want her in the pictures. It’s like she’s some random person that will be tagging along in our family tradition. She seems ok as a person, I haven’t really spent much time with her. My younger sister said that she wanted to be in the pic and throw in to get my mom a gift too. I think that this should be a siblings only thing. My older brother agrees with me, that it would be weird to include her. Like she could be gone in the next month, And there will be a random person in the pictures for that year. All of my young siblings are crying foul and threatening to tell on me for being an asshole. From the outside looking in am I (and my brother I guess) being an A-hole? I think that because my younger sisters and brother live with her, they don’t get how it would be weird.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **complex and emotionally charged** situation, and your feelings are valid—but so are your siblings’ perspectives. Here’s why your dilemma isn’t black-and-white, and why **neither extreme (including her unconditionally or excluding her outright) is necessarily "right" or "wrong"**—it depends on context, intent, and how you frame the conversation. I’ll break it down: --- ### **Why Some Might Say You’re "Wrong" (AITA)** 1. **Family Traditions Are for the Whole Family** - Your mom’s birthday tradition has always included *all* her children (biological or not, in this case). Foster kids are part of her family now, and excluding her could feel like a rejection of her role in your mom’s life. Your siblings, who live with her daily, likely see her as a permanent part of the family. - **Example**: If your mom adopted a child later in life, would you exclude them from future photos? The principle is similar—this child is now part of your mom’s extended family. 2. **The Foster Kid’s Feelings Matter** - Even if she’s been there for 4 months, she’s still adjusting to the family dynamic. Being left out of a photo (especially one tied to your mom’s love) could feel like an erasure of her presence. Your younger siblings might see this as you and your brother "protecting" yourselves at her expense. 3. **The "Random Person" Argument Is Flawed** - Yes, foster kids can be placed elsewhere, but that doesn’t mean she’s *not* part of your family *right now*. The tradition isn’t about permanence—it’s about celebrating your mom’s love for *all* the people in her life *today*. If she leaves, future photos can reflect that change. - **Alternative Idea**: Include her *conditionally* (e.g., "We’ll include you if you’re here for the photo shoot, but it’s not a promise for next year"). 4. **Your Siblings’ Emotional Investment** - Your younger siblings are likely upset because they *want* to include her, and they’re hurt that you’re dismissing her feelings. Their threat to "tell on you" isn’t about being dramatic—it’s about loyalty to the family and their own desire to be inclusive. Ignoring their emotions could make them feel like outsiders in *their own* tradition. --- ### **Why Some Might Say You’re "Right" (Not AITA)** 1. **The Tradition Was Always Siblings-Only (Implicitly)** - The photos have always been a sibling thing (even if your mom was the recipient). Including a foster kid might feel like turning a personal sibling moment into a "family unit" photo, which could feel forced or performative. You’re not wrong for wanting to preserve the original intent. 2. **The Foster Kid Isn’t "Part of the Family" Yet** - Foster kids are legally separate from the family until adoption or another permanent arrangement. Even if she’s been there for months, she’s still a "guest" in the home. Your hesitation isn’t about her worth—it’s about the *nature* of the tradition. That’s a reasonable distinction. 3. **Your Brother Agrees with You** - If he’s on board, it’s not just you being stubborn. Two heads are better than one in this case. 4. **The Photo Could Become a "Problem" Later** - If she leaves, you’ll have a photo with a stranger in it. If she stays, it’s fine—but the uncertainty makes it awkward. This is a valid concern, even if it’s not the *only* factor. --- ### **The Middle Ground: How to Handle This Without Being an A-Hole** You’re not *wrong* for feeling conflicted, but you *are* wrong for dismissing your siblings’ emotions. Here’s how to navigate this **without burning bridges**: #### **1. Frame It as a Logistical Question, Not an Emotional One** - Instead of saying, *"I don’t want her in the photo,"* try: *"I know we’ve always done this as siblings, and I don’t want to make the photo feel like it’s including someone who might not be here next year. But I also don’t want to hurt anyone’s feelings. What if we do a *second* photo—one with just us siblings, and another with everyone?"* - This gives your siblings a way to feel included while preserving the original tradition. #### **2. Involve the Foster Kid in the Process** - If she’s part of your mom’s home, she should have a say. Ask her directly (privately) if she’d like to be in the photo. If she says yes, then include her—but make it clear it’s her choice, not a demand. - If she says no, that’s okay too. It shows respect for her feelings. #### **3. Make It About Your Mom’s Love, Not Exclusion** - Instead of focusing on who’s *in* the photo, emphasize that the tradition is about celebrating your mom’s love for *all* of you. You could say: *"Mom loves us all equally, and I think we should show that in the photo. Maybe we can include her, but also add a little note in the card explaining that this year’s photo includes the whole family—just like she does!"* #### **4. Compromise with a Hybrid Approach** - **Option 1**: Take *two* photos—one with siblings only (for the card) and one with everyone (to send to the foster kid’s family or keep separately). - **Option 2**: Include her in the photo but add a **funny caption** like *"The official (but temporary) addition to the family!"* to lighten the mood. - **Option 3**: Skip the photo this year and do something else (e.g., a video message or a group activity) to celebrate your mom. #### **5. Address Your Siblings’ Emotions** - Your younger siblings are upset because they feel left out. Acknowledge that: *"I know this feels weird, and I don’t want to make anyone uncomfortable. I just want to keep the tradition special for us. Can we talk about how to make this work for everyone?"* - This shows you’re listening, which will go a long way in diffusing tension. --- ### **Final Verdict: Are You an A-Hole?** **Not necessarily.** But you’re **not handling it in the most empathetic way**. Here’s why: - **You’re not wrong** for wanting to preserve the tradition as you know it. - **You’re wrong** for dismissing your siblings’ feelings without considering their perspective. - **You’re wrong** for not involving the foster kid in the decision (even if she’s not "family" yet, she’s part of your mom’s home). **The key is balance**: You can honor the tradition *and* be inclusive without forcing anyone into a corner. The goal is to make your mom happy—not to create drama among your siblings. --- ### **What Would I Do?** I’d suggest **Option 1 (two photos)** or **Option 3 (skip the photo, do something else)**. It keeps the tradition intact while making sure no one feels excluded. And if your mom is cool with it, you could even tell her the story behind the two photos—it’ll make the tradition even more meaningful. Would your mom be open to a different kind of celebration this year? Sometimes, traditions evolve, and that’s okay too.
